questions.question: Which Y-chromosome haplogroup is most commonly associated with Indigenous Amerindian genetics according to the article?
options: Y-chromosome haplogroup Q1a3a
Y-chromosome haplogroup Q-M242
Mitochondrial DNA haplogroup A
Y-chromosome haplogroup R1b
answer_explanations: Correct. The Genetics section states that 'The haplogroup most commonly associated with Indigenous Amerindian genetics is Y-chromosome haplogroup Q1a3a.'
Incorrect. Q-M242 is mentioned in relation to Na-DenÃ©, Inuit, and Indigenous Alaskan populations, but it is not identified as the most commonly associated haplogroup overall.
Incorrect. The article discusses mtDNA but does not identify any specific mtDNA haplogroup as most commonly associated with Indigenous Amerindian genetics.
Incorrect. Haplogroup R1b is not mentioned in the article at all.

questions.question: What does the article say about the timing of human settlement in the Americas?
options: Human settlement occurred in stages from the Bering Sea coastline, with an initial 20,000-year layover on Beringia for the founding population.
Humans settled the Americas in a single rapid migration around 13,000 years ago.
The first people arrived in the Americas approximately 40,000 years ago by boat directly from Asia.
Settlement began only after the end of the last ice age, roughly 10,000 years ago.
answer_explanations: Correct. The Genetics section states: 'Human settlement of the Americas occurred in stages from the Bering Sea coastline, with an initial 20,000-year layover on Beringia for the founding population.'
Incorrect. The article describes settlement as occurring in stages, not as a single rapid migration, and notes debate over dates ranging from 40,000 to 13,000 years ago.
Incorrect. The article describes entry via the Bering Land Bridge and possibly along the coast, not a direct boat migration from Asia.
Incorrect. The article describes human presence well before 10,000 years ago, including sites claimed to date back 20,000 years.

questions.question: What does the article say about the Na-DenÃ©, Inuit, and Indigenous Alaskan populations?
options: They exhibit haplogroup Q-M242 mutations and are distinct from other Indigenous peoples with various mtDNA mutations.
They are genetically identical to other Indigenous peoples of the Americas.
They were the first populations to migrate into the Americas via the Bering Land Bridge.
They lack Y-chromosome DNA entirely, unlike other Indigenous groups.
answer_explanations: Correct. The Genetics section states that these populations 'exhibit haplogroup Q-M242 (Y-DNA) mutations, however, and are distinct from other Indigenous peoples with various mtDNA mutations.'
Incorrect. The article explicitly states they are distinct from other Indigenous peoples, not genetically identical.
Incorrect. The article suggests these populations derived from later migrants into the northern extremes, not that they were the first to migrate.
Incorrect. The article discusses their Y-chromosome mutations, indicating they possess Y-chromosome DNA.

questions.question: What does the article say about the Clovis culture?
options: It was one of the earliest identifiable cultures, with sites dating from some 13,000 years ago.
It was the first and only culture to inhabit the Americas.
It emerged approximately 40,000 years ago in South America.
It was a Mississippian culture centered at Cahokia.
answer_explanations: Correct. The Peopling of the Americas section states: 'One of the earliest identifiable cultures was the Clovis culture, with sites dating from some 13,000 years ago.'
Incorrect. The article describes Clovis as one of the earliest identifiable cultures, not the only one, and mentions older claimed sites.
Incorrect. The article dates Clovis sites to about 13,000 years ago, not 40,000, and places them in North America rather than specifically South America.
Incorrect. The Mississippian culture and Cahokia are discussed separately and appeared around 1000 CE, millennia after Clovis.

questions.question: What does the article say about the short chronology theory of migration to the Americas?
options: It proposes that the first movement beyond Alaska into the Americas occurred no earlier than 14,000â17,000 years ago.
It proposes that the first people entered the hemisphere 30,000â40,000 years ago or earlier.
It argues that humans reached Cape Horn 20,000 years ago.
It claims that the Inuit arrived no more than 2,000 years ago.
answer_explanations: Correct. The article states that under the short chronology theory, 'the first movement beyond Alaska into the Americas occurring no earlier than 14,000â17,000 years ago, followed by successive waves of immigrants.'
Incorrect. The 30,000â40,000 years ago timeframe is associated with the long chronology theory, not the short chronology theory.
Incorrect. The article mentions artifacts dated to 14,000 years ago and human presence at Cape Horn by that time, not 20,000 years ago under the short chronology theory.
Incorrect. The article suggests the Inuit arrived separately no more than 2,000 years ago, but this is not part of the short chronology theory definition.

questions.question: What does the article say about Paleo-Indian bands during much of the Paleo-Indian period?
options: They are thought to have subsisted primarily through hunting now-extinct giant land animals such as mastodon and ancient bison.
They practiced intensive maize agriculture and built large earthen mounds.
They lived in permanent cities with complex stratified societies.
They relied primarily on fishing and coastal resources throughout North America.
answer_explanations: Correct. The Lithic stage and early Archaic period section states: 'During much of the Paleo-Indian period, bands are thought to have subsisted primarily through hunting now-extinct giant land animals such as mastodon and ancient bison.'
Incorrect. Intensive maize agriculture and large earthen mounds are associated with the Mississippian culture, not Paleo-Indian bands.
Incorrect. Paleo-Indian bands are described as small, mobile groups of 20 to 50 members, not permanent cities.
Incorrect. While some groups may have used coastal routes, the article emphasizes hunting megafauna as the primary subsistence strategy during much of the period.

questions.question: What does the article say about Watson Brake?
options: It was a large complex of eleven platform mounds constructed beginning in 3400 BCE and added to over 500 years.
It was the oldest mound complex, built about 1500 BCE in the Lower Mississippi Valley.
It was built by agricultural societies with stratified hierarchies and ceramics.
It was constructed by the Mississippian culture around 1000 CE.
answer_explanations: Correct. The Middle Archaic period section states: 'Watson Brake, a large complex of eleven platform mounds, was constructed beginning in 3400 BCE and added to over 500 years.'
Incorrect. Poverty Point, not Watson Brake, was previously thought to be the oldest mound complex and was built about 1500 BCE.
Incorrect. The article states Watson Brake was built by hunter-gatherer societies, changing earlier assumptions that complex construction required agriculture, sedentism, and ceramics.
Incorrect. Watson Brake dates to 3400 BCE, long before the Mississippian culture which appeared around 1000 CE.

questions.question: What does the article say about the Woodland period?
options: It lasted from roughly 1000 BCE to 1000 CE and refers to prehistoric sites between the Archaic period and the Mississippian cultures.
It was characterized by massive changes occurring in a short period of time.
It began around 1000 CE and featured the construction of Cahokia.
It was defined by the exclusive use of bows and arrows, with no spears or atlatls.
answer_explanations: Correct. The Woodland period section states it 'lasted from roughly 1000 BCE to 1000 CE' and 'refers to prehistoric sites between the Archaic period and the Mississippian cultures.'
Incorrect. The article states the period is 'considered a developmental stage without any massive changes in a short period but instead has a continuous development.'
Incorrect. Cahokia is associated with the Mississippian culture, which appeared around 1000 CE, not the Woodland period.
Incorrect. The article states some Woodland people continued to use spears and atlatls until the end of the period when they were replaced by bows and arrows.

questions.question: What does the article say about the fate of Mississippian groups after the de Soto expedition?
options: By the time Europeans returned a hundred years later, nearly all of the Mississippian groups had vanished.
They successfully resisted Spanish conquest and maintained their cities unchanged.
They migrated en masse to Mesoamerica to join the Aztec Empire.
They formed an alliance with the de Soto expedition and expanded their territory.
answer_explanations: Correct. The Mississippian culture section states: 'By the time Europeans returned a hundred years later, nearly all of the Mississippian groups had vanished, and vast swaths of their territory were virtually uninhabited.'
Incorrect. The article describes disastrous results, disease fatalities, and social disruption, not successful resistance.
Incorrect. There is no mention of migration to Mesoamerica or joining the Aztec Empire.
Incorrect. The expedition suffered losses and arrived in Mexico as a fraction of its original size; no alliance or Mississippian expansion is described.

questions.question: What does the article say about Monks Mound?
options: It remains the largest earthen construction of the prehistoric Americas.
It was built by Paleo-Indian hunter-gatherers around 13,000 years ago.
It was destroyed by European colonizers shortly after 1492.
It is located in the Andes and was part of the Incan Empire.
answer_explanations: Correct. The Mississippian culture section states: 'Monks Mound, the major ceremonial center of Cahokia, remains the largest earthen construction of the prehistoric Americas.'
Incorrect. Monks Mound is associated with the Mississippian culture at Cahokia, not Paleo-Indian hunter-gatherers.
Incorrect. The article does not state that Monks Mound was destroyed by Europeans; it says it remains the largest earthen construction.
Incorrect. Monks Mound is located at Cahokia near modern East St. Louis, Illinois, not in the Andes.
